objective: Serve historical records from the loaded games and box scores: a summary of every record with its holder, and each record's full ranked list, computed live at read time in a bounded number of queries, measured at full-load scale against a stated latency ceiling, so the Stats > Records tab can show them.
acceptance_criteria: The records are a fixed, named set, each with an id, a group (team or player), a title, a unit and a rule text: team-championships (NBA titles won), team-best-season and team-worst-season (regular-season win percentage, then wins), team-most-points-game (points by one team in one game), team-largest-win (margin of victory in one game), player-championships (titles won: a played line for the champion in that season's NBA Finals), player-points-game, player-rebounds-game, player-assists-game and player-threes-game (one player in one game), player-career-points (regular-season points, summed) and player-career-triple-doubles (regular-season games with 10 or more in at least three of points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks).

Counting rules, each named in the record's rule text: single-game records count `regular` and `playoffs` games only (not play-in or the NBA Cup final) and each entry names its game type; season records count `regular` games only and only seasons with a champion (a season in progress never holds a season record); championships use the same NBA Finals rule as GET /events/seasons/{season}/champion, by construction (one shared helper); career records count played rows of `regular` games; every response states the data window as since_season (the earliest stored season) and through_season (the latest).

GET /events/records returns { since_season, through_season, records: [{ id, group, title, unit, rule, holder }] } in the fixed order team records then player records; holder is the first-ranked entry (as in the list below) or null when no stored data qualifies; ties for first return the first by the list's order and a tied_count of how many share the value.

GET /events/records/{record_id}?limit=&offset= returns { id, group, title, unit, rule, since_season, through_season, total, entries } with limit defaulting to 25 (1-100) and offset 0-99; a list holds at most its top 100 entries and total is at most 100; each entry has rank (competition ranking: equal values share a rank, the next rank skips), value, the team (id, name, abbreviation) or the player (id, first and last name) and, where it applies, the season, the game (id, date, game type, opponent abbreviation) and the team the player played for; entries are ordered by value (descending for every record except team-worst-season, ascending), then by date or season, then by id ascending (a record with no date or season, such as a count or a career sum, goes straight from value to id).

An unknown record id is a 404, a limit or offset out of range a 422, and every route's docstring says so, so it reaches openapi.json; an empty database answers 200 with null holders and empty lists, never a 500.

Each value is computed in Postgres (GROUP BY, window functions or ORDER BY ... LIMIT), never by loading box-score or game rows into Python; GET /events/records is built in at most 12 queries and each list in at most 3, whatever the data's size, pinned by query-count tests.

Correctness against a synthetic fixture: for every record, the holder and the first five entries equal values the test derives independently from the fixture rows (including a tie, a DNP line, a play-in game, a cup-final game and a season with no champion that must be excluded).
Indexes are allowed, in one Alembic migration with a downgrade, only where a measurement shows they are needed; the migration and the measurement before and after are in the PR.

Baseline (declared by the skeptic, 2026-10-23; ceilings are medians of 20 warm calls over HTTP after 3 discarded calls, the method of 0x02-events.md's table): (a) bounded lists, pinned by route tests: every ranked list holds at most its top 100 entries (ties at the 100th place are cut by the list's order), total is min(qualifying, 100), limit is 1-100 (default 25), offset is 0-99 and a larger offset is a 422, so no call can page past the 100th entry; (b) query counts, pinned by query-count tests run on two fixture sizes (the correctness fixture, and the same fixture with every season copied three times) giving identical counts: GET /events/records in at most 13 queries (the data window plus one per record) and each GET /events/records/{record_id} in at most 3, for any limit and offset; (c) no Python-side aggregation: no route in app/events/records.py iterates over box-score or game rows; every value, rank and tied_count comes from Postgres (a test asserts the summary fetches at most 12 + 1 result rows per record query, via a cursor row-count listener); (d) scale: measured on a database of at least 29,000 games and 800,000 box-score rows; the PR and 0x02-events.md state whether it is the real load or the synthetic generator, the machine, and pg_relation_size of player_game_stats and games; (e) latency on the local Docker Postgres used for 0x02's table, unconstrained: GET /events/records at most 250 ms; GET /events/records/player-career-points at most 150 ms at limit 25 and at limit 100; every other record's list at most 50 ms at limit 25 and at limit 100, player-career-triple-doubles included; (f) latency on a db.t4g.micro proxy (the same Postgres 16 container run with --cpus=1 --memory=1g and -c shared_buffers=256MB -c work_mem=4MB): GET /events/records at most 500 ms and player-career-points at most 350 ms, recorded only, other records not required; (g) reads, recorded per record in the PR from EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of each of its queries: only player-career-points may read player_game_stats in full (a Seq Scan or full index scan of it); every other record's list query touches at most 2,000 shared buffers (hit plus read); the whole summary touches at most 1.25 x player_game_stats' heap pages plus 4 x games' heap pages; (h) payload, recorded: GET /events/records at most 10 KB and a limit-100 list at most 40 KB; (i) regressions: every existing events route in 0x02's table keeps its median within 10 % or 3 ms, whichever is larger, measured in the same session on the same database before and after the migration; (j) indexes: each one in the migration names the record it serves and is justified by that record's EXPLAIN before and after, in the PR; the migration's upgrade time on the full-scale database is recorded and is at most 60 s locally (the Migration Lambda times out at 10 minutes on a t4g.micro); with the real CSVs, the full load's wall time before and after the migration is recorded. A record that misses its ceiling after indexing is reported in the PR and to the human, and is not shipped behind a cache or a stored table (the human, 2026-10-23: that is a separate unit).

If the real load isn't available, backend/scripts/generate_scale_fixture.py builds a deterministic synthetic database at that scale (fixed seed, 30 teams, 23 seasons, realistic distributions of points and minutes), idempotent; it uses its own id range (nba_game_id from 9,200,000,000, clear of seed_perf.py's 9,000,000,000-9,199,999,999), runs only when ENVIRONMENT is development or perf, and refuses to run if any stored nba_game_id is below 9,000,000,000 (a real load); it is a dev tool, never run in CI or in production, and documented in 0x02-events.md. When it is used, the PR records its triple-double count, its 50-point games, its DNP share, its rows per game and pg_relation_size, against the real data's expected values (the skeptic's report), and says that correctness at scale is unproven.
openapi.json and schema.d.ts match the backend; every existing events route, schema and query count is unchanged; ruff and mypy pass; the backend test suite passes in the container.
